subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage: I'm Manjula. Last week Shreya Ma'am told me off in front of everyone for talking. I looked at the floor and my cheeks felt hot. “Look at me when I'm speaking to you,” she said, and I couldn't. I wasn't being rude. I felt small and my eyes just ran away. At home my Ajji says looking down shows respect for elders, so I don't know what it looked like to Ma'am. After class she said, “I think you were embarrassed. Next time I'll talk to you quietly.” I felt a lot better.

qa.q: Who told Manjula off in front of everyone?
qa.a: Shreya Ma'am told her off in front of everyone.

qa.q: Why couldn't Manjula look at Shreya Ma'am, and what else might lowered eyes mean?
qa.a: She felt small and embarrassed, so her eyes ran away. Lowered eyes can also show respect, as her Ajji says.

qa.q: What did Shreya Ma'am do next that helped?
qa.a: She named that Manjula was probably embarrassed and promised to talk to her quietly next time.

qa.q: How might Shreya Ma'am have read Manjula's lowered eyes at first?
qa.a: As rudeness or defiance, since she asked Manjula to look at her. After class she read it as embarrassment instead.

grounding: A child looks away when scolded in public, from shame or shyness, not defiance.

subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage: Note from Afreen, Class 4 teacher. Jagdish looked at his shoes and rubbed his ear when I praised his drawing in assembly. Earlier, when I corrected his spelling, he also looked away. His grandfather, who collects him, says looking down is how Jagdish shows respect to elders at home. So this may be respect, or embarrassment at attention, or both. I can't be sure which. Next steps: I will praise Jagdish privately, I won't ask for eye contact, and I will check in with him with a quiet question at the end of the day.

qa.q: Where did Afreen praise Jagdish's drawing?
qa.a: She praised it in assembly.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have felt when he looked at his shoes after the praise, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Likely embarrassment or shyness about public attention. It could also be respect, as his grandfather says looking down is how he shows respect to elders.

qa.q: What did Afreen decide to do next?
qa.a: To praise Jagdish privately, to stop asking for eye contact and to check in with a quiet question at the end of the day.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's grandfather see the lowered eyes?
qa.a: As a sign of respect, since he says that is how Jagdish greets elders at home.

grounding: A child looks away when praised or corrected, from shyness or shame, and in some families as respect.

subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage: Diary, Friday. Avni here. Reena Ma'am called my name in assembly today because my poem won. Everyone turned round. I couldn't look up. I stared at the shoelace of the girl in front and felt my ears burn. After, Pooja said, “You didn't even look at Ma'am. That's so rude.” I wasn't being rude! I was so happy and so shy that my eyes wouldn't go up. At home I told Nani, and she said, “In my village we lowered our eyes to teachers anyway. It was respect.” Maybe next time I'll look up for one second and then down again.

qa.q: Why did Reena Ma'am call Avni's name?
qa.a: She called Avni's name because Avni's poem won.

qa.q: Why couldn't Avni look up in assembly?
qa.a: Avni felt happy but very shy with everyone turning round, so the lowered eyes came from shyness, not rudeness.

qa.q: What small step does Avni plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: Looking up for one second and then down lets Avni show thanks to Reena Ma'am without feeling overwhelmed.

qa.q: How did Pooja read Avni's lowered eyes?
qa.a: Pooja saw rudeness, not knowing Avni was shy and that, as Nani said, lowered eyes can show respect.

grounding: Shows a child looking away when praised in public out of shyness, not defiance, and lowered eyes to elders as a sign of respect.

subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage: Disha had three raw mangoes in her frock pocket when Lalit Chacha came round the side of the cowshed. “Whose tree are those from?” Disha stared at the dust by her feet. She said nothing. “Look at me when I'm speaking!” Her chin sank lower, and her toes curled. Dadi, shelling peanuts on the charpai, spoke up. “Lalit, she's not being stubborn. Look how red her ears are. She's ashamed.” Lalit crouched so he wasn't towering. “Disha. Were they from the Patil tree?” A tiny nod. “Then we'll take them back together, and you'll say sorry.” Disha looked up, just for a second.

qa.q: How many mangoes did Disha have?
qa.a: Disha had three raw mangoes in her frock pocket.

qa.q: What did Disha's lowered eyes and curled toes show?
qa.a: They showed she felt ashamed at being caught, not defiant, as Dadi pointed out from her red ears.

qa.q: What changed when Lalit crouched down?
qa.a: By lowering himself and asking a simple question, he made it easier for Disha to answer and to agree to return the mangoes.

qa.q: Why might Lalit have read Disha's silence as stubbornness?
qa.a: Not meeting his eyes looked to him like refusing to listen, so at first he missed the shame behind it.

grounding: Shows a child looking away when caught out, a sign of shame rather than defiance, and an elder helping an adult read it.

subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage: In the Helsinki classroom, Liam read his answer aloud: “Twelve.” Ms Ulla Virtanen shook her head gently. “Not quite. Look again at the second line.” Liam's eyes slid away to the window, to the snow on the bike racks. He didn't look back. A classmate muttered, “He's ignoring her.” Ms Virtanen watched his face: pink, jaw tight, eyes blinking at the glass. She walked over and crouched by his desk, looking at his workbook rather than at him. “It's just the carry. Here.” Liam's eyes came back to the page. “Oh. Fourteen,” he whispered.

qa.q: What answer did Liam first read aloud?
qa.a: Liam first read aloud the answer twelve.

qa.q: What does Liam looking at the window suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt embarrassed at being corrected in front of the class, not that he was ignoring the teacher.

qa.q: How did Ms Virtanen help Liam come back to the task?
qa.a: She crouched beside him and looked at the workbook rather than his face, which took away the pressure and let him try again.

qa.q: How did the classmate who muttered read Liam's look?
qa.a: The classmate took it as ignoring the teacher, missing the pink face and tight jaw that showed embarrassment.

grounding: Shows a child averting the gaze when corrected in class out of embarrassment, not defiance, and a teacher easing the pressure.

subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage:
"Jatin, you skipped warm-up again." Coach Parveen's voice carried across the kabaddi mat.

Jatin stood still, eyes fixed on his toes, hands behind his back.

The new assistant coach, Mr Rego, stepped closer. "Look at the coach when she's talking. Don't be cheeky."

Jatin's ears went red, but his eyes stayed down.

Coach Parveen held up a hand. "Jatin, tell me what happened."
"Sorry, Coach. The bus was late, I came running. I didn't want to interrupt."

Later she told Mr Rego quietly, "His father once told me that at home, looking down at an elder means respect. And he was ashamed. It wasn't cheek."

qa.q: Why did Jatin say he missed warm-up?
qa.a: The bus was late, he came running, and he didn't want to interrupt.

qa.q: What was Jatin most likely feeling as he kept his eyes on his toes?
qa.a: Ashamed and embarrassed at being called out in front of everyone, as his reddening ears suggest; looking down may also be the respect he learned at home.

qa.q: What did Coach Parveen do that worked better than demanding eye contact?
qa.a: She asked Jatin what happened, which brought out the real reason, and later explained the lowered eyes to Mr Rego in private.

qa.q: Why might Mr Rego have read Jatin's lowered eyes differently?
qa.a: Mr Rego expects eye contact as a sign of listening, so lowered eyes looked like cheek; he didn't know what they meant in Jatin's family.

grounding: It shows a child looking away when corrected out of shame and learned respect, and a coach seeing it is not defiance.
